findings.finding: The Maven cache volume (`~/.m2`) has an underspecified lifecycle: the plan does not state whether it is a named Docker volume or a host bind-mount, and it does not specify a retirement/cleanup path. If it is a named Docker volume attached to the compose project, `docker compose down -v` (the always-run teardown step) destroys it on every run, defeating the stated persistence purpose. If it is a host bind-mount, it accumulates indefinitely with no cleanup step. Additionally, the plan provides no concurrency ownership rule for the case where a developer manually triggers a second CI run while a weekly run is still in progress — two `atlas-run` processes writing Maven artifacts to the same cache simultaneously can produce partial-write corruption (Maven's local repo locking is advisory, not atomic across processes).

scenarios: CI: a weekly cron run and a simultaneous `workflow_dispatch` run both reach the Maven download phase and write to the same named volume concurrently — partial artifact writes leave the cache in a corrupt state, causing subsequent runs to fail with mysterious Maven resolution errors that look like network faults.

findings.finding: The new GitHub Actions job in `external-integration.yml` does not declare a `permissions:` block. In a public GitHub repository, jobs inherit the repository's default token permissions (which can include `contents: write`, `packages: write`, `pull-requests: write`, etc.), granting the job's `GITHUB_TOKEN` more privilege than it needs. The job performs only Docker build/run and pytest — it requires at most `contents: read`. An over-broad OIDC token is a least-privilege gap on a CI credential that crosses the GitHub API boundary.
findings.location: Scope section — `.github/workflows/external-integration.yml` new job; AC: 'gains a SEPARATE amd64 job that builds the Dockerfile, waits on the readiness probe, runs only `tests/external/live_jira_dc/`'
scenarios: If the `langfuse-trace` model job also lacks a `permissions:` block (or inherits broad defaults from the workflow-level), the new job silently receives write-level `GITHUB_TOKEN` grants it does not use, increasing blast radius if the job's steps are ever supply-chain-compromised (e.g., a compromised Docker base image exfiltrating the token).

A public-repo workflow with default write permissions is flagged by GitHub's own 'token permissions' CodeQL / workflow hardening advisories, which may trigger automated security alerts for the repository.
findings.suggested_fix:
Add a `permissions` block to the new job definition:
```yaml
jobs:
  jira-dc-integration:
    permissions:
      contents: read
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    ...
```
This matches GitHub's own hardening guidance (GHSA / Actions security best-practices) and is consistent with declaring the job's access posture explicitly, which the T5c criterion requires.

findings.finding: The persistent Maven cache mount is described as 'SHOULD' in plan prose but is absent from all Acceptance Criteria, making it easy for an implementer to omit it. Without the volume mount, every CI run (or local re-run after `docker compose down -v`) re-downloads ~900 Maven artifacts. The plan's own readiness default of 20 minutes was calibrated partly assuming the cache is present on repeat runs; on a cold cache with a slow Maven mirror the 20-minute window could be insufficient, producing flaky timeout failures that look like harness bugs.
findings.location: Scope section (compose file bullet) and AC for compose service settings; plan prose: 'The fixture SHOULD mount a persistent Maven cache (~/.m2) as a volume'
scenarios: Weekly CI cron run on a fresh GitHub runner (cold cache): ~900 artifact download may exceed 20 minutes on a slow Maven mirror, causing the readiness probe to expire with a misleading 'harness not ready' message.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Evaluate and explicitly accept or reject the multi-stage Docker build pattern (prefetch Maven artifacts at image-build time via `mvn dependency:go-offline` or equivalent) as a way to eliminate the hard runtime egress dependency on `maven.atlassian.com` — currently the plan identifies this as 'the real fragility' but does not document why it cannot be addressed structurally.
evidence: 'If Atlassian withdraws the 8.17.1 artifacts from their public Maven repo, the harness stops working despite our pinned base digest. That, not the image, is the real fragility'
The plan's mitigation is a pointer to ticket 9895-ac7d-4276-4f08 (real-instance validation) rather than an evaluation of whether the egress dependency is eliminable at the harness level.

Multi-stage Docker builds with offline Maven prefetch (e.g., `mvn dependency:go-offline -f pom.xml`) are a well-established pattern for converting Maven-at-runtime to Maven-at-build-time, and `atlas-run`'s dependency set is knowable since it is logged (~917 artifacts).
ABSENCE: No section of the plan addresses or rejects a 'fatter image that pre-bakes the artifact download.'
findings.finding: The plan identifies maven.atlassian.com availability as 'the real fragility' of the harness, yet does not evaluate the known prior-art pattern of pre-baking the Maven dependency cache into the image during a multi-stage Docker build (a `mvn dependency:go-offline` or equivalent prefetch stage). This pattern would convert the hard runtime egress dependency into a one-time build-time download, eliminating both the egress requirement on CI runners and the maven.atlassian.com withdrawal risk. The plan accepts the fragility and points to a separate ticket rather than assessing whether it can be structurally removed.
findings.location: Approach section — 'Four consequences the harness must design around' / 'If Atlassian ever withdraws…'
scenarios: Atlassian removes the 8.17.1 plugin artifacts from maven.atlassian.com (already noted as a real risk since Atlassian ended DC sales), silently breaking the harness on every future run.
A CI runner's egress is restricted for security reasons, making the harness unrunnable in that environment even with a pinned base image.

The plan's own AC requires the harness to 'start' and 'prove REST v2 answering,' but a pre-baked image would be far more reliable as an acceptance oracle than one that depends on a third-party CDN being available at test time.

findings.finding: The plan asserts 'the PAT bearer auth the DC transport uses is exercised for real' and the AC requires an `Authorization: Bearer` request to succeed — but the actual adapter code (`AcliRestMixin._direct_rest_get`, `_direct_rest_put_raw`, `_direct_rest_post_json`, `_direct_rest_delete` in `acli_rest.py`; `acli.py:466,639`; `acli_cli_ops.py:80,423`) uniformly builds `Authorization: Basic <base64(user:api_token)>` for every REST call. There is no `Bearer` header anywhere in the transport layer. The PAT AC exercises a mode the actual DC transport never uses — it is a test of a hypothetical future auth mode, not the current one. Evidence class: Contradicted (code directly falsifies the 'DC transport uses Bearer' claim).
findings.location: Approach section ('PAT bearer auth the DC transport uses is exercised for real'); Testing section ('auth path: a Personal Access Token minted on the 8.17.1 instance authenticates a request via Authorization: Bearer'); AC ('a PAT-authenticated request succeeds'); AC ('The PAT is created programmatically by the fixture via POST /rest/pat/latest/tokens... the resulting token is then used in an Authorization: Bearer request')
